Family Health

Bleeding after sex when you have an IUD

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Bleeding after sex can feel alarming when you rely on an IUD. Many causes are treatable, but the device should not be used as an automatic explanation. The pattern of bleeding, associated symptoms and an examination help determine what is happening and whether any change to your contraception is needed.

Bleeding after sex deserves its own explanation

An IUD can change your periods, but bleeding specifically during or after sex is a separate symptom worth discussing with a clinician. It may come from irritation, dryness or another treatable problem. Do not assume that being within the first few months after insertion explains every episode, or that a settled device rules out another cause.

Contact a primary-care or sexual-health service even if the amount is small. Tell them whether this was a single episode, is happening repeatedly, or comes with pain or discharge. Being assessed does not mean you necessarily need the IUD removed. It helps distinguish ordinary cycle changes from bleeding that needs treatment.

What the two kinds of IUD do

An intrauterine device is a small contraceptive placed inside the uterus by a trained professional. Common models are T-shaped. Copper devices work without hormones; hormonal devices release a progestogen and are also called intrauterine systems, or IUSs. Both are highly effective: fewer than one user in a hundred becomes pregnant in the first year of typical use.

Neither type prevents sexually transmitted infections. Condoms reduce that risk, and testing may still be needed. A copper device can also provide emergency contraception, commonly when inserted within five days of unprotected sex. A clinician can assess timing, including circumstances in which timing from ovulation is relevant.

Replacement dates depend on the actual device

Keep the device name, insertion date and agreed replacement date. There is no universal twelve-year lifespan for every copper coil or three-to-five-year limit for every hormonal coil. For example, NHS guidance describes copper products lasting five or ten years and hormonal products lasting three to eight years. Available products and approved or guideline-supported use differ between countries.

The reason for use also matters. A hormonal device used to protect the uterine lining during hormone replacement therapy may have a different replacement schedule from one used only for contraception. Ask the fitting service to confirm your own date rather than extending it based on another person’s device.

Expected period changes are different for each type

Cramping and spotting can follow insertion. With a copper IUD, periods may become longer, heavier or more painful, sometimes with period-related backache. These changes are often most noticeable in the first three to six months and may improve, but a return to the old pattern at exactly six months is not guaranteed.

A hormonal IUD commonly causes irregular light bleeding early on. Over time, periods often become lighter or stop. The chance of having no bleeding varies by product and duration; it is not the same fixed percentage for everyone. Heavy or prolonged bleeding is less typical with a hormonal device. Report troublesome bleeding, a new change after a settled pattern or symptoms such as marked tiredness instead of waiting out a calendar deadline.

Other symptoms should not all be labelled side effects

Some hormonal-device users report headaches, acne, breast tenderness or mood changes. A symptom beginning after insertion does not by itself prove the device caused it. Weight changes can have several explanations, and evidence does not establish that an IUD causes weight gain. Discuss symptoms that persist or affect your wellbeing.

Small ovarian cysts can occur with hormonal devices and often disappear without treatment. Pelvic pain still needs its own assessment: it should not automatically be attributed to a cyst or to hormonal adjustment. New or severe pain, particularly with fever, bleeding or unusual discharge, calls for prompt advice.

Pain during sex or changed threads needs a position check

Pain with penetration can have several causes, including a device that has moved. Arrange a check if your threads feel different, you cannot feel threads you could previously find, your partner notices them, or you feel the hard device. Missing threads sometimes curl into the cervix or uterus; they do not prove that the IUD has fallen out.

If its position is uncertain, avoid vaginal sex or use condoms until assessed. Ask promptly about emergency contraception after recent sex because the best option depends on timing and the device. Do not pull the threads, push a low device upward or attempt to reposition it yourself.

Possible causes include the cervix, vagina and nearby tissues

Friction against dry or inflamed tissue can cause small surface injuries. Vulvovaginitis means inflammation around the vulva and vagina. Cervicitis is inflammation of the cervix and can be related to an infection, including an STI. Cervical ectropion exposes delicate glandular cells on the outside of the cervix; these can bleed when touched. Cervical polyps are small growths that are usually benign.

Bleeding near the beginning or end of a period may happen to coincide with sex, and pregnancy is another possibility. Less often, cervical or other gynaecological cancer needs investigation. Ordinary intercourse does not reach the inside of the uterus: do not assume that bleeding represents an injury to its lining. Blood noticed after sex might also come from external skin or the urinary opening, so mention pain when urinating or uncertainty about where it began.

After menopause, even one episode should be checked

Lower oestrogen can make vaginal tissue thinner and more easily irritated. This is a common explanation for postmenopausal bleeding, but it cannot be confirmed from the amount or colour alone. Polyps, changes in the uterine lining and cancers are other possibilities. Arrange assessment even for one small spot or pink or brown discharge.

A hormonal IUD can stop periods before menopause, so absent bleeding on its own does not establish that menopause has occurred. Tell the clinician about your device and any hormone therapy. Neither an IUD nor a recent normal cervical screening result removes the need to investigate new symptoms.

What a consultation and examination may involve

Bring the device details and a brief record of bleeding, pain, discharge and the last usual period. The clinician may offer a pregnancy test and infection tests using a swab or urine sample. With your consent, a speculum examination lets them see the vaginal walls and cervix. A separate examination with fingers inside the vagina and a hand on the abdomen can assess tenderness or masses. You can ask for a chaperone, explanation or pause.

Cervical screening checks for HPV or cell changes according to the local programme; it is not a complete diagnostic test for bleeding. Depending on age and findings, further assessment might include ultrasound, a closer cervical examination called colposcopy, or investigation and sampling of the uterine lining. Everyone does not need every test. Ask how results will arrive and what to do if symptoms recur before then.

Treatment follows the cause and your preferences

Dryness may improve with a suitable lubricant, vaginal moisturizer or prescribed treatment for hormonal tissue changes. Reduce painful friction while the area heals. Infection needs the correct medicine and sometimes partner testing or treatment. A symptomatic polyp may be removed; suspected cancer requires specialist assessment and an individual treatment plan.

A displaced IUD may need removal or replacement by a professional. If bleeding is a device effect and you want to keep it, ask about management options; you can also choose another contraceptive method. There is no universal two-week break from sex that treats every cause. Follow the specific healing or infection advice and arrange reassessment if bleeding continues.

When to seek urgent or emergency help

Seek prompt medical advice for a positive pregnancy test with an IUD, possible pregnancy with pain or bleeding, fever, offensive discharge or very heavy bleeding. Pregnancy with an IUD is uncommon, but its location must be checked. Do not delay because a pregnancy test has not yet become positive if concerning symptoms are present.

Severe or worsening abdominal pain, shoulder-tip pain, fainting or collapse can indicate a ruptured ectopic pregnancy or another emergency. Seek emergency care, especially with bleeding or possible pregnancy. Ongoing heavy blood loss with weakness or dizziness also needs urgent help rather than a routine contraceptive appointment.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Expected menstrual changes and bleeding linked specifically to sex need separate consideration.

Investigation should account for pregnancy, infection, device position and cervical or uterine causes.

How BeMama can help

Record the device name and symptoms, arrange a check and agree on a plan that fits your contraceptive preferences.

When to seek help

Severe pain, shoulder-tip pain, fainting or heavy bleeding with weakness needs emergency assessment. Possible pregnancy with pain or bleeding needs urgent advice.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Ask for an assessment of bleeding after sex, even with a recently fitted IUD.
  • Copper and hormonal devices affect menstrual bleeding differently.
  • Missing or changed threads need a position check and temporary contraceptive precautions.
  • Bleeding after menopause should be investigated even when it happens only once.
  • Treatment and replacement timing depend on the cause, product and your preferences.

Frequently asked questions

Should I wait six months before reporting bleeding after sex?

No. The early adjustment period describes common menstrual changes, not a reason to ignore contact bleeding. Arrange a check sooner, particularly for pain, recurrent episodes, unusual discharge or heavy bleeding.

Can an IUD cause painful sex?

Pain can occur if the device has moved, but dryness, infection and other conditions can also cause it. A clinician can examine you and check the device. Do not try to move it yourself.

What if I cannot feel the threads?

Use condoms or avoid vaginal sex and contact the clinic promptly. The threads may have retracted, but protection cannot be assumed until assessed. Ask about emergency contraception if you have had recent sex.

Does a normal cervical screening result rule out the cause?

No. Screening and investigating symptoms serve different purposes. A normal result does not explain new bleeding, so tell the clinician when it started and whether it keeps happening.

Do all copper IUDs last twelve years?

No. Duration depends on the product, local guidance and sometimes circumstances at insertion. Check the recorded replacement date with your clinician; do not extend it by applying another device’s lifespan.

Is no period on a hormonal IUD dangerous?

It can be an expected effect of thinning the uterine lining. An abrupt change with pregnancy concerns or other symptoms may still need a pregnancy test or assessment. It does not prove menopause.

Will I definitely need the IUD removed?

No. A treatable cause may be unrelated to the device. Removal or replacement is considered if needed or if you prefer it, with a plan for ongoing contraception.

Could the blood be from somewhere other than the uterus?

Yes. The cervix, vaginal wall, external skin or urinary tract can be involved. Tell the clinician about surface soreness, painful urination or uncertainty about where the blood came from.

Can I use lubricant and skip the appointment?

Lubricant may reduce dryness or friction, but it does not establish the cause of unexplained bleeding. Arrange assessment and avoid activity that causes pain while awaiting advice.

Is one small spot after menopause worth checking?

Yes. Even a single small episode needs assessment. Dry tissue is one possible explanation, but other cervical or uterine causes need to be considered.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
